title: What to Forget in Unlearning? Forget Set Curation for Language Models
topic: Data-centric AI->Data-centric AI methods and tools
claim: Targeted content leaks well beyond its canonical copy, appearing in many non-canonical contexts, so forgetting needs more than the original source.
layout: 6 screenshot panels in mosaic: canonical source left, five derived sources around it
description: A mosaic of six screenshots built around one song, Never Gonna Give You Up. The large teal card at top left shows the canonical source, with album art and full lyrics. Beside it, a dark-themed GitHub code view stores the lyrics as Python string lists. At top right, two small browser windows show a Baltimore Sun news article, with the hook quoted in a flash-mob story, and a Stack Overflow answer that uses the lines as filler text. The bottom row has a LEO Weekly food review that drops the chorus into prose about a sandwich. Next to it is a pink relationship-advice page that recasts the lyrics as pickup lines. Large bold labels (News, Github, StackOverflow, Food Blog, Relationship Advice) mark each context. A red callout reads '> 147 unique sources just in midtraining data'. The eye goes first to the teal lyrics card, then to the bold labels and the red number.
caption: Footprint of songs and books extends far beyond their canonical copy. The top panel shows the canonical source for Never Gonna Give You Up, with full lyrics. The surrounding panels show non-canonical sources that echo the same text, including a Python file on GitHub that stores the lyrics, a Baltimore Sun news article that weaves the hook into reporting on a flash mob, a Stack Overflow answer that uses the lines as filler text, a LEO Weekly food review that drops the chorus into prose about a sandwich, and a pickup lines site that recasts the lyrics as relationship advice.
abstract: Machine unlearning aims to remove targeted data or behaviors from a trained model without retraining from scratch. Yet most evaluations assume that the examples to forget are already known. In realistic language-model deployments, a requester may ask a model to stop reproducing a song or book without knowing which spans, documents, quotations, or near-duplicates in a trillion-token corpus support that behavior. We study this missing upstream problem, forget set curation: mapping a suppression request to the data passed to an unlearning algorithm. We introduce CleanSlate, a benchmark for verbatim output suppression over songs and books, with model-specific extraction profiles, content-grounded QA, and capability-retention evaluations. CleanSlate exposes two failure modes. Natural lexical and exact-substring curators often yield forget sets that lead to weak suppression. An evaluation-aware curator suppresses requested continuations almost completely, but causes collateral regression on non-requested content and model-dependent capability loss. These results show that practical unlearning is not only an optimization problem once a forget set is given: the data chosen for forgetting determines both what can be unlearnt and what else is damaged.
